passage: At the community-centre chess club, Yash moved his queen and sat back, pleased. Coach Manoj studied the board, pushed his tongue into his cheek so it bulged, and said, “Brilliant move, grandmaster.” The older kids snorted. Yash beamed. Then the girl opposite took his queen with a pawn, and the snorting got louder. Yash's face crumpled; he looked from the board to the coach's bulging cheek. Manoj stopped smiling and pulled a chair over. “Sorry, Yash. That face is my joke face; the older ones know it. It wasn't fair when you didn't. Let's look at what the pawn could do.”

qa.q: What took Yash's queen?
qa.a: The girl opposite took his queen with a pawn.

qa.q: What was Yash feeling when he looked from the board to the coach's cheek?
qa.a: He felt confused and embarrassed, realising the praise may have been a joke that everyone else understood.

qa.q: What did Manoj do to repair things?
qa.a: He apologised, explained that the bulging cheek was his joke face that only the older kids knew, and helped Yash look at the pawn's move.

qa.q: How did the older kids read the coach's bulging cheek?
qa.a: They knew from shared experience that it meant a joke, so they snorted instead of taking the praise seriously.

grounding: Shows a tongue pressed in the cheek signalling a joke to those who share the context, and confusing a child who does not.

passage: I'm Bhavna, and I share a desk at home with my brother Darshan. Every evening, when he does long division, his tongue pushes into his left cheek until there's a lump like a marble. Yesterday Papa walked past and frowned. “What's so funny, Darshan? Are you making faces at your homework?” Darshan looked up, tongue still in cheek, then quickly pulled it back. “No, Papa.” I can't see inside his head, but I've watched that lump appear over every hard sum for two years, and it never comes with a laugh. I told Papa, “That's his thinking lump.” Papa looked again and nodded slowly.

qa.q: Which cheek does Darshan's tongue push into?
qa.a: His tongue pushes into his left cheek.

qa.q: What was Darshan likely feeling when Papa asked what was funny?
qa.a: He was probably startled and a bit embarrassed, since he was concentrating on long division, not joking.

qa.q: How did Bhavna help Papa read the face?
qa.a: Bhavna shared two years of watching the lump appear over hard sums, giving Papa the context he lacked.

qa.q: Why might Papa read the tongue in cheek as a joke?
qa.a: Papa may know the look as a sign of hiding a joke, and hadn't seen that Darshan does it while concentrating.

grounding: Shows a child pressing the tongue into a cheek while concentrating, misread as hiding a joke by someone without the shared context.

passage: Saturday: After Preeti's dance at the family function, her cousin Bidisha Didi said, “Worst dance I've ever seen,” with her tongue pushed into one cheek. Preeti's eyes stung, and she hid in the kitchen. Sunday: Bidisha found her on the terrace. “Yesterday, did you see my cheek? That lump means I'm joking. I thought you knew. Your dance was great.” Preeti frowned. “Then just say it was great.” “Fair. I'll say it straight with you.” Wednesday: Bidisha burned the rotis. Preeti pressed her tongue into her cheek and said, “Best rotis in the world.” Bidisha burst out laughing.

qa.q: Where did Bidisha find Preeti on Sunday?
qa.a: Bidisha found her on the terrace.

qa.q: What was Preeti feeling after the comment on Saturday?
qa.a: Preeti felt hurt, her eyes stinging, because she took the words literally without knowing the joke signal.

qa.q: What did the cousins agree, and why was it sensible?
qa.a: Bidisha agreed to say things straight to Preeti, since a joke signal only works when both people share it.

qa.q: What was Wednesday like for Bidisha?
qa.a: Bidisha found it funny to get her own joke face back over the burnt rotis, which showed they now shared the signal 😄

grounding: Shows a tongue-in-cheek joke signal hurting a child who didn't share the context, and working once the meaning is shared.

subtype: Blank face at bullying or shame [Regulating]
passage: Note to the school counsellor, Tuesday. Vandana, Class 6. This is the third time I've seen a group near the water cooler comment on Nandini's cracked shoes. Each time her face goes completely still: no frown, no tears, eyes fixed somewhere past them, as if she can't hear. Today I asked her to help me carry books to the staff room. There I said, “I've noticed the comments. You don't have to act like they don't hurt. I can help.” She kept the same blank face for a moment, then said, “They do it every day.” I spoke to the group this afternoon. Please see Nandini before home time. Counsellor's reply, below: Seeing her at 2:30 today.

qa.q: What has the group been commenting on?
qa.a: The group has been commenting on Nandini's cracked shoes.

qa.q: What was Nandini most likely feeling behind her still face?
qa.a: She was most likely hurt and ashamed by the daily comments, keeping her face still so the group got no reaction.

qa.q: What steps did Vandana take, and why do they help?
qa.a: Vandana checked in privately, said Nandini didn't have to pretend and offered help, then spoke to the group and asked the counsellor to see Nandini that day.

qa.q: Why might the group think the comments don't matter?
qa.a: Because Nandini's face showed nothing, they might believe she didn't care, so the blank look hid how much it hurt.

grounding: Shows a child keeping a blank face under teasing to avoid giving a reaction, and a teacher checking in privately and getting help the same day.

subtype: Blank face at bullying or shame [Regulating]
passage: Monday. Irfan's diary. In the bus line today Rohit's gang called me “Aloo” again and puffed their cheeks out. I did my stone face, like always. Nothing moves, not even my eyebrows. If I don't react, they get bored. Only Avni noticed. At lunch she said, “Your face goes like a wall. Same as when Sir shouted at you.” I didn't answer. But tonight I told Ammi everything, even about the wall face. She put her tea down and sat on my bed. She said it's not my fault, and I don't have to hold the wall up with her. She messaged my class teacher right then, and Ma'am replied that she'll speak to the gang first thing. Ammi checked on me again before lights out.

qa.q: What did Rohit's gang call Irfan?
qa.a: They called Irfan “Aloo” and puffed their cheeks out.

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling behind the stone face?
qa.a: Irfan was hurt and embarrassed by the teasing, and kept the face still hoping the gang would get bored.

qa.q: How did Ammi respond, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She listened, said it wasn't Irfan's fault and messaged the class teacher that night, so the teasing will be dealt with and Irfan isn't alone with it.

qa.q: What did Avni notice that others missed?
qa.a: Avni saw that the still face was a wall, the same one Irfan made when upset before, so it hid hurt rather than showing Irfan didn't care.

grounding: Shows a child keeping a blank face under teasing to hide hurt, and a trusted adult responding the same evening with help.

subtype: Blank face at bullying or shame [Regulating]
passage: At the village school near the paddy fields in Goa, the boys at the back had a new song about Francis's patched shorts. Francis sat with his face flat as a slate, eyes on the blackboard, hands still on the desk. He didn't blink when a paper ball hit his ear. Hansa Teacher saw it land. She didn't make a scene. At the lunch bell she asked Francis to help her fill the water pot at the well. There she said, “A face can stay very still when something hurts. You can tell me.” His jaw tightened, then let go. He told her. That afternoon she kept the back row behind and sent a note home to Francis's mother.

qa.q: What hit Francis's ear?
qa.a: A paper ball hit his ear.

qa.q: What was Francis likely feeling behind his flat face?
qa.a: He was likely hurt and humiliated by the song, keeping his face still so the boys got no reaction.

qa.q: How did Hansa Teacher make it safe for Francis to speak?
qa.a: She took him to the well away from the others and told him a still face can hide hurt and that he could tell her.

qa.q: What would change if Hansa had scolded the boys in front of everyone at once?
qa.a: Francis might feel even more exposed and might not tell her what had really been happening.

grounding: Shows a child keeping a rigid, blank face while teased, and a teacher checking in privately and acting the same day.

passage: “I can't come to cricket on Sunday,” Francis said, face perfectly flat. “My family is moving to Antarctica.” Farhan stopped chewing. “What? When?” “Tomorrow. We're taking the goat.” “Francis. Are you serious? You never said!” “Very serious. The goat has a coat already.” Farhan's eyes went shiny. “But… who'll bowl with me?” Francis cracked. “Farhan! I'm joking! We're going to my aunty's wedding.” “Then why didn't your face do anything?” “That's what makes it funny.” “Not for me! Give me a sign or something.” Francis thought. “Okay. When I'm joking, I'll tap my nose.” He tapped it. “Like that.”

qa.q: Where did Francis say his family was moving?
qa.a: Francis said his family was moving to Antarctica.

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling when his eyes went shiny?
qa.a: Farhan felt upset and worried about losing his cricket partner, because he took the flat face as serious.

qa.q: What small signal did the boys agree on, and why does it help?
qa.a: Francis will tap his nose when joking, which lets Farhan know it's deadpan humour without spoiling the joke.

qa.q: Why does Francis think the flat face makes it funny?
qa.a: For Francis the joke works because the face gives nothing away, and he hadn't realised Farhan couldn't tell.

grounding: Shows a child's deadpan joke confusing a friend, and a small signal agreed to show it is a joke.

passage: I'm Ujjwal, and I used to think my straight face was my best joke. Last term, when our teacher asked what we'd done at the weekend, I said, with no smile at all, “I trained my cat to do my homework.” Half the class laughed. Anjali, who'd just moved from Bhopal, wrote it in her notebook. At break she asked me, very seriously, how I trained it. I felt awful and funny at the same time. Now, when I tell a deadpan joke, I let one eyebrow go up at the end, just a little. Anjali calls it my joke flag. She laughs at the right time now.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal claim the cat had been trained to do?
qa.a: Ujjwal claimed the cat had been trained to do homework.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling when Anjali asked how the cat was trained?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt awful and amused at once, realising the joke had fooled a newcomer who didn't know the style.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal change, and why does it work?
qa.a: Ujjwal now lifts one eyebrow at the end of a deadpan joke, a small signal that lets newcomers know it's a joke.

qa.q: What was the joke like for Anjali as a newcomer?
qa.a: Anjali didn't know Ujjwal's style yet, so she took it seriously and even wrote it down, which may have felt confusing later.

grounding: Shows deadpan humour being funnier for those who know the style but confusing a newcomer, and a small signal fixing it.

passage: Class note, Friday. Harish, Class 5. Kiran's deadpan humour is brilliant and sometimes gets Kiran into trouble. At today's science demo, when the volcano failed, Kiran said, “As planned. That was the quiet version,” without a flicker. The class roared. The visiting examiner didn't laugh, and wrote “disrespectful” on the sheet. I know Kiran meant no harm. The class knows the style; a stranger doesn't. After the lesson I told Kiran the joke was good and asked for a small signal for new people: a grin at the end, or a glance at me. Kiran chose the grin and tried it at lunch.

qa.q: What did Kiran say when the volcano failed?
qa.a: Kiran said, “As planned. That was the quiet version.”

qa.q: What was the visiting examiner likely feeling when Kiran spoke?
qa.a: The examiner was likely offended or puzzled, reading the flat face as rudeness because the deadpan style was unfamiliar.

qa.q: What did Harish suggest, and why?
qa.a: Harish asked for a small signal, like a grin at the end, so strangers can tell the deadpan remark is a joke.

qa.q: How does the class see Kiran's humour?
qa.a: The class knows Kiran's style, so they find the flat delivery funnier, unlike a stranger.

grounding: Shows a child's deadpan humour delighting those who know the style but confusing a stranger, and a small signal to show it's a joke.

subtype: Bowing the head and namaste in India [Mismatch]
passage: On the morning the chief guest arrived, the children of Class 4 lined up at the school gate. When Neelam Madam, a retired headmistress, stepped out of the car, Bidisha pressed her palms together, dipped her head and said, “Namaste, Madam.” Beside her, Emma, the exchange student from Australia, looked worried. “Is Bidisha in trouble? She's looking at the ground.” The class teacher smiled. “No, it's a greeting. See how her back is straight and she's smiling? When someone bows their head in shame, the shoulders drop and there's no smile.” Emma watched, then tried a small namaste herself. Neelam Madam returned it to both of them.

qa.q: Where had Emma come from?
qa.a: Emma was the exchange student from Australia.

qa.q: What was Emma feeling when she saw Bidisha look at the ground?
qa.a: Emma felt worried that Bidisha was in trouble, reading the bowed head as shame.

qa.q: How did the teacher help Emma tell the two apart?
qa.a: The teacher pointed to Bidisha's straight back and smile, contrasting them with dropped shoulders and no smile in shame.

qa.q: What might the greeting mean to Neelam Madam?
qa.a: To Neelam Madam it probably felt like warm respect, which she showed by returning the namaste 🙏

grounding: Shows a child bowing the head with namaste as respect, and how it differs from head-bowing in shame.

subtype: Bowing the head and namaste in India [Mismatch]
passage: I'm Gopika, and I stand next to Rashmi in Bharatanatyam class. At the start, every girl touches the floor and does a namaste to our teacher, head dipped. Rashmi's bow is always neat and quick, chin tucked, eyes up again at once, and she smiles. Last Thursday she lost the rhythm twice in the new piece. The teacher said, “Again, Rashmi. Watch the count.” Rashmi's head went down again, but differently: slowly, and it stayed down. Her shoulders curled. Her feet stopped. I can't say what she was feeling. But it didn't look like the first bow at all. After class the teacher went over and spoke to her softly.

qa.q: In which class does Gopika stand next to Rashmi?
qa.a: Gopika stands next to Rashmi in Bharatanatyam class.

qa.q: What might Rashmi's slow, lingering bow after the correction suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt ashamed or discouraged at losing the rhythm, unlike the quick, smiling bow of respect at the start.

qa.q: What could the teacher say to Rashmi after class?
qa.a: The teacher could reassure her that new pieces take practice and help her with the count, so the correction doesn't feel like shame.

qa.q: How does Gopika tell the two bows apart?
qa.a: Gopika notices speed, eyes, smile and shoulders: quick and smiling for respect, slow and curled after the correction.

grounding: Shows a child's head bow with namaste as reverence and a different head-bow in shame, with context deciding the meaning.

subtype: Bowing the head and namaste in India [Mismatch]
passage: Friday: Nikita arrived from Dubai for the summer. At the door, her Dada Ramesh waited. Nikita didn't know what to do, so she hung her head and stared at the floor. “Is she upset?” Dada whispered to Papa. Sunday: On the veranda, Dada showed her. “Palms together, a small dip of the head, then look up and smile. It says, I respect you. Hanging the head says, I'm sorry, or I'm sad.” Nikita practised on the cat. Tuesday: When the neighbour aunty came with sweets, Nikita pressed her palms together, dipped her head, looked up and smiled. The aunty beamed. Dada winked at her from his chair.

qa.q: Where did Nikita arrive from?
qa.a: Nikita arrived from Dubai.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling when she hung her head on Friday?
qa.a: She felt unsure and shy, not knowing the greeting, so her hanging head looked like sadness even though it was confusion.

qa.q: How did Dada's lesson on Sunday help?
qa.a: He showed the difference between a small respectful dip with a smile and a hanging head, giving her a clear way to greet elders.

qa.q: How did Friday's greeting look to Dada Ramesh?
qa.a: It looked to him as if she might be upset, since a hanging head can mean sadness or shame.

grounding: Shows a child learning the namaste with a slight head bow as respect, and how it differs from hanging the head in sadness.

passage: The bell was about to ring, and the corridor was jammed with Class 7 pushing past. Kunal had one minute to explain to Karthik Sir why his project was late. “My printer ran out of ink, and the shop was shut, so I…” Sir tilted his head to one side. Kunal's words tangled. He doesn't believe me. Then he noticed Sir had also leaned closer, one hand cupped near his ear, eyebrows soft. “Say that again? It's so noisy.” Kunal almost laughed. The tilt was for hearing. He repeated it, louder. Sir nodded. “Bring it tomorrow. Thanks for telling me.”

qa.q: Why was Kunal's project late?
qa.a: His printer ran out of ink, and the shop was shut.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling when Sir tilted his head?
qa.a: Kunal felt anxious and doubted, thinking the tilt meant Sir didn't believe him.

qa.q: What cues helped Kunal read the tilt correctly?
qa.a: Sir's leaning closer, the cupped hand near his ear and his soft eyebrows showed he was trying to hear, not doubting.

qa.q: What was the moment like for Karthik Sir?
qa.a: Sir was struggling to hear over the noisy corridor and just wanted Kunal to repeat himself.

grounding: Shows a child reading a teacher's head tilt as doubt, when body cues and tone show listening.

passage: In their Delhi flat, Mridul came out of his room and announced, “Mumma, room's all clean.” Anjali looked up from her laptop and tilted her head to one side. Mridul smiled. She's impressed. Then he noticed the rest: one eyebrow lifted, lips pressed into a small line, and her voice, slow and flat. “Oh, really? All clean?” He shifted his feet. His cricket kit was still on the bed, and the socks were under it. “Mostly clean,” he said. Anjali's head straightened and she laughed. “Mostly. Go finish, and then I'll come and see.”

qa.q: What was still on Mridul's bed?
qa.a: His cricket kit was still on the bed.

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling when he first saw the head tilt?
qa.a: He felt pleased and hopeful, thinking she was impressed, before the other cues made him uneasy.

qa.q: Which cues told Mridul the tilt meant doubt?
qa.a: The lifted eyebrow, pressed lips and slow, flat voice showed that the tilt meant doubt, not admiration.

qa.q: How did Anjali see Mridul's announcement?
qa.a: Anjali doubted the room was really clean and used a teasing tone to let him admit it himself.

grounding: Shows a child reading a parent's head tilt, first as interest, then as doubt once the eyebrow and tone are added.

passage: “And then they changed the group chat name so I wasn't in it anymore.” Ankita stopped. Sarita Ma'am had tilted her head to one side. “You don't believe me,” Ankita said quickly. “Why do you say that?” “Your head. My tuition teacher does that when she thinks I'm making excuses.” “Ah.” Sarita Ma'am kept her voice low and warm. “For me it means I'm listening hard. It sounds like that really hurt.” Ankita looked at her face again: soft eyes, no frown, leaning in. “It did.” “Thank you for telling me. Let's work out together what we can do about it today.”

qa.q: What did the group change so Ankita wasn't in it?
qa.a: They changed the group chat name so Ankita wasn't in it anymore.

qa.q: Why did Ankita think Sarita Ma'am didn't believe her?
qa.a: Ankita felt anxious and defensive, because her tuition teacher tilts her head like that when she doubts excuses.

qa.q: What helped Ankita read the tilt differently?
qa.a: Sarita Ma'am explained what the tilt meant for her, and her soft eyes, warm voice and leaning in backed it up.

qa.q: What was Sarita Ma'am trying to show with the tilt?
qa.a: She was trying to show she was listening closely and felt sympathy for how hurt Ankita was.

grounding: Shows a child reading a teacher's head tilt as doubt, when tone and body show sympathy and listening.

passage: I'm Chandrika, from the flat opposite, and I was watering my tulsi when Farhan came up the stairs after the badminton final. His racket hung from one hand. His shoulders had sunk so low his school bag slid off one side, and he didn't hitch it back. His mother opened the door. “Cheer up, beta, it's only a game!” she said brightly. Farhan's shoulders dropped even more. His grandfather, behind her, said nothing at first. He just took the bag and said, “Three sets in that heat. Tiring, and disappointing.” Farhan leaned into him. I don't know what he felt, but his shoulders came up a little.

qa.q: How many sets did Farhan play?
qa.a: Farhan played three sets in the heat.

qa.q: What do Farhan's sinking shoulders suggest after the final?
qa.a: They suggest he felt sad and defeated after losing, too low even to hitch his bag back up.

qa.q: Why did the grandfather's words help more than “Cheer up”?
qa.a: He named the effort and the disappointment warmly, so Farhan felt understood instead of told to hide his feeling.

qa.q: How does Chandrika read Farhan's mood?
qa.a: Chandrika only sees the sunk shoulders and the lean into his grandfather, and doesn't claim to know his feelings.

grounding: Shows a child's dropped shoulders after a loss, and a warm word helping more than being told to cheer up.

passage: Monday: Pooja walked out of the school gate holding her maths test, 38 out of 50, and her shoulders slumped so low her bag straps slipped. Her brother Chinmay, waiting on his cycle, said, “Oh, stop sulking. Chin up!” Pooja's shoulders sank further, and she walked home without a word. Wednesday: Chinmay knocked on her door. “Sorry about Monday. I got a worse mark in Class 6. You studied every night; I saw. It's okay to feel rubbish about it.” Pooja's shoulders loosened. Saturday: Pooja brought her fractions book to Chinmay's desk. “Will you check these?” She sat up straight while he did.

qa.q: What mark did Pooja get on her maths test?
qa.a: Pooja got 38 out of 50.

qa.q: What was Pooja feeling when her shoulders slumped at the gate?
qa.a: She felt disappointed and defeated by the mark, after studying every night.

qa.q: What did Chinmay change on Wednesday, and why did it work?
qa.a: He apologised, shared his own worse mark and said it was okay to feel rubbish, which gave warmth instead of an order to cheer up.

qa.q: What was Monday like for Chinmay?
qa.a: Chinmay may have meant to help, but his quick “Chin up” made his sister feel worse, which he realised later.

grounding: Shows a child's dropped shoulders after disappointing marks, and a warm word helping more than telling her to cheer up.

passage: Karthik, you asked why I still keep that old bronze medal. Listen, then. I, your Aparna Athai, was eleven and sure I'd win the district race. I came third. When I walked off the track, my shoulders fell so low I felt shorter. My father met me at the gate and said, “Enough long face. Smile, people are watching.” I tried, and it felt like swallowing a stone. Then my coach, Mrs Pillai, sat beside me on the bench. She didn't tell me to smile. She said, “You wanted gold badly, and you ran your hardest. It's allowed to hurt.” I cried on her shoulder. The next year, I ran again.

qa.q: Where did young Aparna come in the district race?
qa.a: Aparna came third.

qa.q: What was young Aparna feeling as she walked off the track?
qa.a: She felt deeply disappointed and defeated, her shoulders falling so low she felt shorter.

qa.q: What choice did Mrs Pillai make, and why did it matter?
qa.a: She didn't ask for a smile but named Aparna's effort and hurt, which let her cry and later run again.

qa.q: How might Aparna's father have felt about his words?
qa.a: He probably wanted to protect her pride in front of others, not realising that asking for a smile made her feel worse.

grounding: Shows a child's dropped shoulders after a loss, and a warm word helping far more than being told to smile.

passage: At recess in their Singapore school, Mei handed Noa a folded invitation. “My birthday, Saturday. Will you come?” Noa read it and lifted one shoulder, just a little. Mei's smile wobbled. That's a no. She doesn't want to. She almost took the card back. Then she remembered her mum saying a shrug can mean a hundred things. “Is that a yes, a no or an I don't know?” Noa looked at her shoes. “I want to. It's just, it's a sleepover, and I've never slept away from home.” “Oh! You could come for the cake and go home before bed?” This time both of Noa's shoulders went up, in a happy bounce.

qa.q: What day was Mei's birthday party?
qa.a: Mei's birthday party was on Saturday.

qa.q: What was Mei feeling when Noa lifted one shoulder?
qa.a: Mei felt hurt and disappointed, reading the small shrug as a no.

qa.q: What did asking reveal?
qa.a: It showed Noa wanted to come but felt nervous about sleeping away, so they found a way she could join for the cake.

qa.q: What was the invitation like for Noa?
qa.a: Noa felt torn, wanting to go but nervous about a first night away from home, which the half-shrug showed.

grounding: Shows a child reading a friend's one-shoulder lift as a no, and asking to find it meant uncertainty.

passage: At the Sunday football club, Deepak, captain for the day, needed a goalkeeper. “Deepika, will you go in goal?” Deepika lifted one shoulder and looked sideways at the posts. Deepak nearly shouted, “Great, go!” and ran off to sort the others. Then he stopped. One shoulder wasn't really a yes. “Is that a maybe?” Deepika rubbed her arm. “Last time I dived, I scraped my whole elbow. And everyone saw when I let in three.” Deepak thought. “Do the first half as defender, then? Asha can start in goal.” Deepika nodded, properly this time, and jogged to the back.

qa.q: How many goals did Deepika let in last time?
qa.a: She let in three.

qa.q: What was Deepika feeling when she lifted one shoulder?
qa.a: She felt nervous and unsure, remembering the scraped elbow and everyone seeing the three goals.

qa.q: Why was asking “Is that a maybe?” wise?
qa.a: A one-shoulder lift is a weak signal, so asking brought out her worry and let Deepak offer a better position 👍

qa.q: What would change if Deepak had taken the shrug as a yes?
qa.a: Deepika might have gone in goal feeling scared and embarrassed, and Deepak would never have learned why she hesitated.

grounding: Shows a child reading a teammate's one-shoulder lift as a half-hearted maybe, and asking to clarify it.

passage: I'm Yogesh, and I sit with Baljeet in the back row. Yesterday Baljeet asked the new girl, Ritu, if she wanted to join our quiz team. Ritu lifted one shoulder and kept her eyes on her pencil box. Baljeet turned to me. “See? She's not interested.” I didn't know either. It could have meant anything. But Baljeet went back and asked, “Is that a no, or are you just not sure yet?” Ritu said quietly, “I'm not good at quizzes. I didn't want to let you down.” Baljeet said we mostly just guess anyway. She laughed and joined. I don't know what made Baljeet go back, but I'm glad.

qa.q: What did Baljeet ask Ritu to join?
qa.a: Baljeet asked Ritu to join their quiz team.

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling when she lifted one shoulder?
qa.a: Ritu felt unsure and worried about letting the team down, not uninterested.

qa.q: Which of Baljeet's choices worked, and why?
qa.a: Going back and asking what the shrug meant worked, because it brought out Ritu's worry so it could be answered.

qa.q: How did Yogesh read the shrug?
qa.a: Yogesh wasn't sure and thought it could mean anything, so there was no easy answer for Baljeet.

grounding: Shows a child reading a new classmate's one-shoulder lift as disinterest, then asking and finding shyness and doubt.

passage: When the flower pot outside the staff room was found smashed, Uma Ma'am walked down the corridor asking questions. Tarun stood by the notice board with both hands behind his back, very still. Two children glanced at him. Uma Ma'am slowed. Hands hidden, standing stiff. It would have been easy to decide. Instead she asked, “Tarun, did you see what happened to the pot?” “No, Ma'am. I was in the library.” His ears were pink. “What are you holding?” He brought his hands round slowly: a folded card with glitter, “Happy Teachers' Day” on the front. “It was for tomorrow. It's a surprise.” Uma Ma'am's face softened.

qa.q: What was written on the front of the card?
qa.a: “Happy Teachers' Day” was written on the front.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling as he stood with his hands behind his back?
qa.a: He was probably nervous about being suspected, and also shy about his surprise card being found.

qa.q: Why was Uma Ma'am's approach fair?
qa.a: She didn't treat hidden hands as proof and asked plain questions, which revealed an innocent surprise.

qa.q: How might the two children who glanced at Tarun read his hands?
qa.a: They might have assumed he was hiding something to do with the broken pot, since hidden hands can look guilty.

grounding: Shows a child's hands behind the back signalling concealment of something innocent, and why the pose is not proof of guilt.

passage: I'm Payal. At the Independence Day parade, Pema stood in front of me in the line, hands clasped behind her back, chin up, feet apart, exactly as the PT teacher showed us. She looked proud. On Monday I saw her again, outside the principal's office, and her hands were behind her back again. But this time her fingers were twisting together, and she kept shifting from one foot to the other. The office helper said, “What has she done?” I said I didn't know. Later she told me she'd been called in to hear she'd won the essay prize. Same hands. Totally different Pema.

qa.q: Where did Payal see Pema on Monday?
qa.a: Payal saw Pema outside the principal's office.

qa.q: What was Pema likely feeling outside the principal's office?
qa.a: She was likely nervous, twisting her fingers and shifting her feet, not knowing why she'd been called.

qa.q: What lesson could the office helper take from this?
qa.a: That hands behind the back don't prove someone has done something wrong, and waiting to find out is fairer.

qa.q: How does Payal compare the two poses?
qa.a: Payal notices that the same hands meant pride at the parade but nerves outside the office, shown by the twisting fingers and shifting feet.

grounding: Shows a child's hands behind the back meaning respect at a parade and nervousness elsewhere, and not proof of guilt.

passage: Saturday: Harish arrived at Vandana Dadi's house and stood in the doorway, hands locked behind his back. Dadi frowned. “What have you broken this time?” “Nothing!” His face went red. Sunday: At the temple, when the priest spoke to him, Harish stood the same way, hands behind, back straight. Dadi watched. It was how the school made them stand for assembly, Papa explained. Just manners. Dadi felt a small pinch of guilt about Saturday. Tuesday: Harish came in with his hands behind his back again. Dadi only smiled and waited. He held out a jar of tamarind sweets. “Your favourite,” he said, grinning.

qa.q: Where did Harish stand the same way on Sunday?
qa.a: At the temple, when the priest spoke to him.

qa.q: What was Dadi feeling after Papa's explanation on Sunday?
qa.a: Dadi felt a small pinch of guilt about accusing Harish on Saturday, realising the pose was manners.

qa.q: What did Dadi do differently on Tuesday, and why was it better?
qa.a: She smiled and waited instead of assuming he had broken something, which let the surprise gift come out.

qa.q: How might Harish have felt when Dadi asked what he'd broken?
qa.a: He likely felt hurt and embarrassed, since he'd done nothing and was only standing politely.

grounding: Shows a child's hands behind the back meaning respect, then a surprise, and a grandparent learning it is not proof of guilt.

passage: On the playground in Edinburgh, Soo-ah was the last to come in from lunch. Ms Freya Campbell stood at the door with both hands on her hips. Soo-ah froze. At her old school, that pose meant trouble. She walked slowly, head down, ready for a scolding. Then Ms Campbell spoke, breathing hard. “Phew! I just ran the three-legged race with Year 4. I'm puffed out.” She was grinning, cheeks pink, and her hands stayed on her hips while she caught her breath. “Come in, Soo-ah. Did you see us fall over?” Soo-ah's shoulders came down, and she laughed.

qa.q: What race had Ms Campbell just run?
qa.a: She had just run the three-legged race with Year 4.

qa.q: What was Soo-ah feeling when she saw the hands on hips?
qa.a: Soo-ah felt scared and ready for a scolding, because at her old school that pose meant trouble.

qa.q: Which cues showed Soo-ah the pose meant resting?
qa.a: Ms Campbell's heavy breathing, grin, pink cheeks and friendly words showed she was catching her breath, not angry.

qa.q: What would change if Ms Campbell had not spoken?
qa.a: Soo-ah might have gone in believing she was in trouble and felt anxious all afternoon.

grounding: Shows a child reading a teacher's hands on hips as impatience when tone and words show she was resting.

passage: At lights-out in the school hostel, Vikas Sir stood at the end of the corridor with his hands on his hips. Simran, still whispering to her bunkmate through the open door, stopped mid-sentence. Hands on hips means he's fed up. Then he spoke, quiet and even: “Ten o'clock. Lights off in two minutes, please.” Not shouting. Not smiling either. Simran studied him: feet planted, voice calm, eyes moving from door to door, counting. It was his in-charge pose, she decided. Not angry, just firm. She switched off her lamp. “Good night, Sir.” “Good night, Simran.”

qa.q: How long did Vikas Sir give before lights off?
qa.a: He gave two minutes before lights off.

qa.q: What was Simran feeling when she first saw the hands on hips?
qa.a: She felt nervous, thinking he was fed up with the whispering.

qa.q: How did Simran work out what the pose meant?
qa.a: She added his calm, even voice, planted feet and counting eyes to the pose, and read it as firm authority, not anger.

qa.q: How might Vikas Sir see his own stance?
qa.a: He probably sees it as a normal way to stand while checking rooms, not as a sign of anger.

grounding: Shows a child reading an adult's hands on hips as impatience, then using tone and words to read it as authority.

passage: I'm Gargi. At kabaddi practice on Tuesday, Coach stood at the edge of the mat with both hands on her hips while Hansa did her raid. Hansa got tagged out, looked over, and her face fell. She walked back slowly, muttering, “She's annoyed with me.” I wasn't sure. Coach's voice, when it came, was cheerful: “Nice footwork, Hansa! Again!” Then Coach pressed her hands into her lower back and stretched, wincing a little. “Old back,” she said. Hansa looked at me. I shrugged. Maybe the hands had just been holding up her back all along.

qa.q: What did Coach say after Hansa's raid?
qa.a: Coach said, “Nice footwork, Hansa! Again!”

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling when she walked back muttering?
qa.a: Hansa felt discouraged and worried that Coach was annoyed with her.

qa.q: What could Hansa do next time she sees that pose?
qa.a: She could wait for Coach's words and tone, or ask, before deciding the hands on hips mean impatience.

qa.q: How did Gargi read Coach's pose?
qa.a: Gargi wasn't sure, and later thought the hands might just have been supporting Coach's sore back.

grounding: Shows a child reading a coach's hands on hips as impatience, when words and tone suggest resting a sore back.

passage: I'm Sonali, Imran's cousin, and I was at the dhaba with his family on Sunday. When the food was late, Imran snapped his fingers at the waiter twice, loudly, the way people do in films. The waiter's face went stiff, and he walked the other way. Imran's Abbu leaned over. “Beta, snapping at someone feels like calling a dog. Say ‘Bhaiya, excuse me.’” Imran went red and nodded. Later, when the parathas came, he rubbed his hands together fast, grinning. The same waiter smiled at that. I think it looked hungry, not rude.

qa.q: How many times did Imran snap his fingers at the waiter?
qa.a: Imran snapped his fingers at the waiter twice.

qa.q: What was Imran feeling when he went red?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed, realising his snap had seemed rude when he only meant to get attention.

qa.q: What did Abbu suggest instead of snapping?
qa.a: He suggested saying “Bhaiya, excuse me,” a polite way to get the waiter's attention.

qa.q: How did the waiter likely feel about the snapping?
qa.a: The waiter probably felt disrespected, as if called rudely, which is why his face went stiff.

grounding: Shows a child snapping fingers to call attention, which seems rude at people, and rubbing hands in eager anticipation.

passage: Monday: During the maths test, Yash snapped his fingers under the desk, soft and steady, counting. Sahil, beside him, hissed, “Stop showing off!” Yash stopped, confused. Wednesday: At break, Yash explained. “The snaps help me count times tables. I wasn't doing it at you.” Sahil shrugged. “It just sounded like hurry up.” They agreed on a tap on the knee instead. Friday: A freezing morning. Sahil sat rubbing his hands together fast, grinning as the teacher handed out the quiz. Yash leaned over. “Cold, or excited?” “Both! I studied all week,” Sahil whispered.

qa.q: What did Yash and Sahil agree on instead of snapping?
qa.a: Yash and Sahil agreed on a tap on the knee instead.

qa.q: What was Yash feeling when Sahil hissed at him?
qa.a: Yash felt confused and a bit hurt, since the snapping was only to help count, not aimed at Sahil.

qa.q: What small step fixed Monday's problem?
qa.a: Explaining the snaps and agreeing on a quiet knee tap let Yash keep counting without it sounding like hurry up.

qa.q: How did the snapping sound to Sahil on Monday?
qa.a: To Sahil it sounded like showing off or telling him to hurry up, not like counting.

grounding: Shows finger-snapping as rhythm being misread, and hand-rubbing carrying both cold and eager anticipation.

passage: Jatin, stop snapping at your sister and listen to your Rukmini Paati. When I was nine, in our village music class, a boy named Selvam snapped his fingers all through the song. Snap, snap, snap. The teacher spun round and hit the desk with her ruler. “Are you calling me like a servant?” Selvam's face went grey. He whispered, “No, Teacher. It's how I keep the beat. My father keeps time that way for his drum students.” The teacher stopped. She asked him to snap again, slowly, while we sang. We all sang in time for the first time that year. After that she let him keep the beat, but never at people.

qa.q: What was Selvam doing all through the song?
qa.a: Selvam snapped his fingers all through the song.

qa.q: What was Selvam feeling when his face went grey?
qa.a: He felt frightened and shocked that his rhythm-keeping was taken as rudeness.

qa.q: What choice did the teacher make after Selvam explained, and why did it matter?
qa.a: She asked him to snap slowly while the class sang, which turned a misunderstanding into help with the beat.

qa.q: How did the snapping first seem to the teacher?
qa.a: To the teacher it seemed like calling her rudely, like calling a servant, until she heard it was keeping time.

grounding: Shows finger-snapping as rhythm-keeping being mistaken for rudeness, and snapping at people being seen as rude.
